newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK analysts warn against overestimation on H-shares.
newsitem.headline: HK analysts warn against overestimation on H-shares.

text.p: Investors are shrugging off disappointing earnings reports from H-share companies and instead snapping up selected stocks in the hope they will soar as China's economy grows, analysts told Reuters.
"The overall H-share results announced so far were disappointing," said Peter So, deputy head of Hong Kong and China research at Schroder Securities.
H-shares are the Hong Kong listings of China-incorporated companies.

The Hang Seng China Enterprise Index, which tracks H-shares, has risen 8.5 percent this year to close at 1,064.75 on Thursday. The blue-chip Hang Seng Index has lost 5.4 percent to 12,726.83 over the same period.
Analysts generally recommend infrastructure, infrastructure related industries and other machinery industries as a buy.
But they warned an expected recovery in China's state companies would come at a slower pace and smaller magnitude than many investors thought.
"We originally expected China's petrochemical sector would recover this year, but it looks pretty unlikely now," Lawrence Ang, head of China research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said.
The industry was likely to be squeezed by a worldwide petrochemical product price slump, analysts said.
Yizheng Chemical Fibre Co Ltd said weak domestic demand and oversupply in 1996 depressed product prices. The company reported prices fell an average 37 percent in 1996 from the previous year.
The polyester products maker posted an 82 percent drop in 1996 net profit to 215.65 million yuan ($26 million).
Oil refiner Zhenhai Refining & Chemical Co Ltd was the only company within the four petrochemical H-shares to report growth in 1996 net profit with a 13.5 percent increase to 592.42 million yuan.
"The petroleum market in China is complicated and the management of Zhenhai successfully proved that they handled the market situation quite well," Ang said.

The management of light truck maker Qingling Motors Co Ltd also earned praise from analysts for an increase in both production and earnings last year in the face of sluggish sales and keen competition in China's vehicle market.
Qingling recorded the best results so far with a 140 percent rise in net profit to 426.29 million yuan.
About half of the 26 H-share companies have reported results, but only four reported earnings growth in 1996.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was considering a downward revision to its average earnings per share growth forecast for H-shares in 1997 to 10 percent or even single digits from the current estimate of 18 percent, Ang said.
"None of (the results) is above our forecast," he said.

Shanghai Hai Xing Shipping Co Ltd lost 157.47 million yuan in 1996 against a 37.65 million profit the year before but its shares have jumped nearly 50 percent since a brief dip on April 16 when it announced its results. The share closed at HK$1.70 on Thursday, up HK$0.19.
Analysts said investors were buying on hopes of asset injections after a reorganisation at its Shanghai parent.
"Many of the H-share companies forecast to show an improvement in earnings in 1997 have risen sharply lately," said Rachel Tsang, manager of China research at Vickers Ballas.
She forecast mild earnings growth of 15 to 20 percent for the machinery and infrastructure sector this year.
"Therefore I prefer to wait for a consolidation before jumping in," Tsang said.
